title: MVCC, locking and concurrency control
scopeHtml: Scope: MVCC, lock types, SELECT FOR UPDATE, deadlocks, advisory locks, optimistic vs pessimistic, safe migrations.

notes.title: MVCC: readers do not block writers
notes.html:
MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) keeps several versions of a row so readers see an old consistent version while a writer builds a new one. Readers never wait for writers and writers never wait for readers; only writer vs writer on the same row waits.

Mechanism in Postgres: an UPDATE does not change a row in place. It inserts a new tuple and stamps the old one's xmax. Each query gets a snapshot: the list of transactions that were committed at that moment (xmin, xmax, and in-progress xids). A tuple is visible if its creator is committed and in the snapshot, and its deleter is not.

heap tuples for one logical row
ctid (0,1)  xmin=100 xmax=210  name='Ann'   <- old, ended by 210
ctid (0,7)  xmin=210 xmax=0    name='Anna'  <- new
Reader with snapshot before 210 commits sees (0,1); after, sees (0,7).

Hint bits and system columns you can inspect:

SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;

Worked example. A 100 GB table gets 1,000 updates/s on random rows. Each update adds ~100 bytes of new tuple, so roughly 100 KB/s, or 8.6 GB/day of new versions, which VACUUM must reclaim (file 09). The cost of MVCC is dead tuples; the benefit is a read-heavy workload that never blocks.

Industry examples. Postgres, Oracle (undo segments) and InnoDB (undo log) all use MVCC with different storage. HOT updates (heap-only tuples) let Postgres skip index updates when no indexed column changes and the new version fits on the same page; fillfactor (e.g. 90) leaves room for that.

Decision gravity. MVCC is baked into the engine; you cannot turn it off. You tune around it: fillfactor, autovacuum, short transactions.

Everyday analogy. A shared document with version history: you keep reading the version from when you opened it while a colleague writes the next one.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying an UPDATE modifies the row in place in Postgres.
  • Forgetting that every extra index must also be updated unless the update is HOT.

notes.title: Lock types in Postgres
notes.html:
Locks are the other half of concurrency control: they stop two writers from corrupting the same thing. Postgres has locks at several levels; most day to day work uses row locks and table locks taken implicitly.

Table-level modes, weakest to strongest (names to know):

  • ACCESS SHARE: taken by plain SELECT.
  • ROW SHARE / ROW EXCLUSIVE: SELECT FOR UPDATE / INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE: VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  • SHARE: CREATE INDEX (non concurrent), blocks writes.
  • ACCESS EXCLUSIVE: ALTER TABLE (most forms), DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL. Blocks everything, even SELECT.

Row-level modes: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE. Row locks live in the tuple header (xmax plus flags), not in a lock table, so locking a million rows does not blow memory, but it does write to the heap.

-- who is waiting for whom
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, state, wait_event_type, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Incident pattern (the lock queue). ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN x int needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. A long SELECT is running, so ALTER waits. Now every new query on users queues BEHIND the ALTER, and the app freezes within seconds, even though only a harmless read caused it. Symptom: sudden connection pile-up, all waiting on Lock: relation. Mitigation: SET lock_timeout = '2s' before DDL and retry, and kill long transactions first.

Industry examples. GitLab, Shopify and Stripe have published rules for safe migrations: lock_timeout, add columns nullable with no default (or constant default on Postgres 11+, which is instant), create indexes concurrently, add constraints NOT VALID.

Everyday analogy. A single-lane bridge closing for repairs: it waits for the current truck to pass, but all new cars line up behind the barrier.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing ALTER TABLE is always cheap.
  • Not setting lock_timeout for DDL in production.

notes.title: SELECT FOR UPDATE and friends
notes.html:
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them so other writers (and other lockers) must wait until you commit. It is the standard tool for read-modify-write and check-then-act when you want certainty without Serializable.

BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;   -- lock row
-- app computes new balance
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 70 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

Variants:

  • FOR NO KEY UPDATE: lock for updates that do not change keys; does not block foreign key inserts that only need FOR KEY SHARE. Plain UPDATE takes this automatically.
  • FOR SHARE / FOR KEY SHARE: block writers but allow other shared lockers.
  • NOWAIT: error immediately if locked.
  • SKIP LOCKED: silently skip locked rows, ideal for job queues.

Job queue with SKIP LOCKED (worked example). 10 workers each claim 50 jobs:

WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'pending'
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 50
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', worker = 'w3'
FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id
RETURNING jobs.*;

No two workers get the same row and nobody waits. Throughput of several thousand jobs/s on one table is typical (illustrative) before you need Kafka or SQS.

Industry examples. Queue libraries built on Postgres (River, Que, GoodJob, pg-boss and others) rely on FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

Everyday analogy. Putting your name on a meeting room whiteboard: others see it is taken and either wait, or (SKIP LOCKED) just pick another room.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking in different row orders in different code paths (deadlock source).
  • Using FOR UPDATE on a large range (locks, bloats the heap with xmax writes).
  • Forgetting the lock lasts until COMMIT, not the end of the statement.

notes.title: Deadlocks
notes.html:
A deadlock is a cycle of waiting: A holds X and wants Y, B holds Y and wants X; nobody can move. Postgres detects it (after deadlock_timeout, default 1 s), aborts one transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01), and the other proceeds.

Session A                           Session B
BEGIN;                              BEGIN;
UPDATE acct SET b=b-10 WHERE id=1;
                                    UPDATE acct SET b=b-10 WHERE id=2;
UPDATE acct SET b=b+10 WHERE id=2;  -- waits for B
                                    UPDATE acct SET b=b+10 WHERE id=1;
                                    -- waits for A: DEADLOCK, one aborted

Prevention:

  1. Consistent lock order. Always touch rows in the same order (e.g. smallest id first). Lock both accounts in one statement: SELECT ... WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE.
  2. Keep transactions short.
  3. Retry on 40P01 (with jitter).
  4. Lock at one coarse level (a guard row) when ordering is hard.

Diagnose: set log_lock_waits = on (logs waits longer than deadlock_timeout); the server log shows both queries involved. pg_stat_database.deadlocks counts them.

Industry examples. Batch jobs that upsert many rows in unordered batches deadlock against each other all the time. Sorting the batch by primary key before INSERT ... ON CONFLICT removes the problem.

Everyday analogy. Two cars meeting on a narrow road, each waiting for the other to back up; a traffic warden forces one to reverse.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a deadlock is a Postgres bug. It is application ordering.
  • Not distinguishing a long wait (lock contention) from a deadlock (cycle).

notes.title: Advisory locks and application-level mutual exclusion
notes.html:
Advisory locks are locks whose meaning YOU define; Postgres just stores the key. Use them to guard things that are not rows: "only one instance runs the nightly job", "only one process migrates tenant 7".

-- session-level, non blocking: returns true if acquired
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42);
-- ... do the work ...
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42);

-- transaction-level: auto released at COMMIT/ROLLBACK
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('tenant:7'));

Rules: keys are 64-bit ints (or two 32-bit ints). Session-level locks survive COMMIT and are tied to the connection, which is dangerous with transaction-mode connection poolers (the lock stays on a pooled server connection). Prefer the xact variants with poolers.

Industry examples. Migration tools (Rails, Flyway, Liquibase-style) take an advisory lock so two deploys do not migrate simultaneously. It is a cheap leader election for small clusters; for multi-database or cross-region locking, use etcd/ZooKeeper/Redis-based locks with fencing tokens.

Decision gravity. Easy to add and reverse. But a lock tied to a single Postgres cannot protect work that spans several systems; a paused process can resume thinking it still holds the lock, so critical effects need a fencing token (monotonic number checked by the resource).

Everyday analogy. A "do not disturb" sign on a door. Postgres only keeps the sign; it is up to everyone to respect it.

Common interview traps.

  • Session-level advisory lock plus PgBouncer transaction pooling (lock leaks or is never released).
  • Treating a lock as proof that no one else is acting (no fencing).

notes.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency
notes.html:
Pessimistic: assume conflict, lock first (FOR UPDATE). Optimistic: assume no conflict, detect it at write time and retry.

Optimistic with a version column:

-- read
SELECT id, title, version FROM docs WHERE id = 5;   -- version = 7
-- write: succeeds only if nobody changed it meanwhile
UPDATE docs
SET title = 'New', version = version + 1
WHERE id = 5 AND version = 7;
-- affected rows 0  => conflict: reload and retry or tell the user

Postgres also exposes the hidden xmin as an ad-hoc version, but an explicit column is clearer and portable. JPA's @Version does exactly this.

Pessimistic Optimistic
Best when Conflicts are common, work is short Conflicts rare, think time is long (user edits a form)
Cost Waiting, deadlocks Retries on conflict
Holds DB resources across user time Yes (bad) No
Failure mode Blocked queue, lock waits Retry storms on hot rows

Worked example. A product page editing form takes 2 minutes. Pessimistic locks would hold a row for 2 minutes (or a transaction open, impossible with pooling). Optimistic: 2 minutes pass with no DB lock, and at save 1 in 200 saves hit a version mismatch and show "someone else changed this". For a hot counter (10,000 increments/s on one row), do neither; use atomic SET n = n + 1, or shard the counter across N rows and sum.

Industry examples. HTTP ETag plus If-Match is optimistic concurrency at the API layer. DynamoDB conditional writes and etcd compare-and-swap are the same idea.

Decision gravity. Choose per entity. Adding a version column later is a cheap migration; mixing both models on the same rows needs care.

Everyday analogy. Pessimistic is reserving the whole library table before you start; optimistic is working freely and checking at the end that nobody replaced your source book.

Common interview traps.

  • Holding a database transaction open while waiting for user input.
  • Optimistic locking on a very hot row (almost everyone retries).

notes.title: Table locks, row locks and lock escalation
notes.html:
Postgres never escalates row locks into table locks. (SQL Server and Db2 do, which can freeze a whole table when one query touches many rows.) Postgres row locks are stored in the tuple itself, so there is no memory pressure to escalate.

Things that DO take table-wide locks and surprise people:

  • Most ALTER TABLE forms (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE); changing a column type usually rewrites the table.
  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY (blocks writes for the duration).
  • VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, TRUNCATE, REINDEX (non concurrent).
  • Foreign keys: INSERT into a child takes FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row.

Safe migration pattern:

SET lock_timeout = '3s';
-- fast metadata-only change; retried by the deploy script on timeout
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
-- build index without blocking writes (cannot run in a transaction)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);
-- add constraint cheaply, validate later
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk CHECK (total >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk;   -- only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE

Worked example. CREATE INDEX on a 200 GB table takes ~30 minutes (illustrative). Non-concurrent version blocks all INSERT/UPDATE for 30 minutes (outage). CONCURRENTLY takes about 2 to 3x longer but only blocks other schema changes. If it fails it leaves an INVALID index you must drop.

Industry examples. Tools like pg_repack and pgroll / online-schema-change helpers exist to avoid ACCESS EXCLUSIVE rewrites.

Everyday analogy. Painting one lane of a road at a time versus closing the whole motorway.

Common interview traps.

  • Running CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction (error).
  • Forgetting an invalid index left behind after a failed concurrent build.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• MVCC: UPDATE writes a new tuple; readers use snapshots, so reads and writes do not block each other.
  • Writers conflict on the same row; row locks live in the tuple, no escalation.
  • Table lock modes range from ACCESS SHARE to ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; a waiting ALTER can block the whole app via the lock queue. Use lock_timeout.
  • FOR UPDATE serialises read-modify-write; SKIP LOCKED makes a Postgres job queue; NOWAIT fails fast.
  • Deadlocks (40P01) come from inconsistent lock order: fix with ordering, short transactions, retries.
  • Advisory locks are app-defined mutexes; prefer transaction-level variants behind poolers; add fencing for critical work.
  • Optimistic (version column, retry) suits long think time; pessimistic suits short hot conflicts; hot counters need atomic updates or sharded counters.

questions.promptHtml: How does MVCC work in Postgres, and what does it cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: MVCC explains locking, vacuum, bloat and isolation; it is the base of every Postgres performance conversation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Postgres never updates a row in place. An UPDATE inserts a new tuple version and stamps the old one's xmax. Each query uses a snapshot of which transactions were committed, so readers see the old version while the writer builds the new one. Readers never block writers and vice versa; only two writers on the same row wait. The cost is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ctid (0,1)  xmin=100 xmax=210  name='Ann'   <- old, ended by tx 210
ctid (0,7)  xmin=210 xmax=0    name='Anna'  <- new
Snapshot before 210 commits sees (0,1); after, sees (0,7).

A tuple is visible if its creator is committed and within the snapshot, and its deleter is not. Extra costs: every index needs a new entry unless the update is HOT (no indexed column changed and room on the same page), so fillfactor around 90 leaves space. Compare Oracle and InnoDB: they update in place and keep old versions in an undo log; Postgres keeps them in the heap, which makes rollback instant but needs vacuum.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying UPDATE modifies in place.
  • Forgetting index maintenance cost when the update is not HOT.
  • Long transactions pin old versions and block cleanup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a HOT update? -> A heap-only tuple update that skips index changes when no indexed column changed and the page has room.
  2. Why is rollback instant in Postgres? -> The aborted xid simply never becomes visible.
  3. What sets the vacuum horizon? -> The oldest snapshot still in use, such as a long transaction or a stale replication slot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "readers do not block writers". Senior: tuple versions, snapshots, HOT, and the operational price in bloat and long transactions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A forgotten idle-in-transaction session kept old versions alive and a 20 GB table doubled in size.

questions.promptHtml: What table-level lock modes does Postgres have, and which statements take the strong ones?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tells if you can predict which DDL or maintenance commands block traffic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Weakest to strongest: ACCESS SHARE (plain SELECT), ROW SHARE and ROW EXCLUSIVE (FOR UPDATE, DML), SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), SHARE (plain CREATE INDEX, blocks writes), and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL), which blocks even SELECT. Row locks are separate and live in the tuple header.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Modes conflict by a matrix; ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with everything. Row-level locks (FOR UPDATE, NO KEY UPDATE, SHARE, KEY SHARE) are stored in xmax plus flags in the tuple, not in shared memory, so locking a million rows does not exhaust a lock table, but it writes to the heap. Lock requests queue in order: a waiting strong lock blocks later weak requests behind it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, state, wait_event_type, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing ALTER TABLE is always cheap.
  • Forgetting that the queue effect makes a waiting lock as damaging as a held one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does plain SELECT block ALTER TABLE? -> It takes ACCESS SHARE, which conflicts with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so yes, a long SELECT makes the ALTER wait.
  2. Which lock does CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY take? -> SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so writes continue.
  3. Where are row locks stored? -> In the tuple header (xmax and infomask), with no escalation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names a few modes. Senior: knows the queueing effect, which commands rewrite, and how to inspect blockers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An innocent ALTER froze checkout for 90 seconds because a report held ACCESS SHARE.

questions.contextHtml:
A team uses a Postgres jobs table as a queue with 10 workers. Duplicate processing is reported: the same job id ran on two workers about 1 in 2,000 times. Each worker runs:

BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;
-- app loops over ids
UPDATE jobs SET status='running', worker='w3' WHERE id = ANY($ids);
COMMIT;

The throughput is only 200 jobs/s. A teammate suggests adding Redis locks.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and what is the better query?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a Redis lock" or "use Serializable", without noticing that nothing locks the selected rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a job processed inside the transaction or after? What is the job duration? Are retries or visibility timeouts needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make jobs idempotent or dedupe by id downstream.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the select takes no row locks, so two workers pick the same pending rows; (b) slow update; (c) network retry (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Two sessions running the select simultaneously return overlapping ids.
  5. Root cause: Read-then-update race in Read Committed.
  6. Fix:
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='pending'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs SET status='running', worker='w3'
FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id
RETURNING jobs.*;

Disjoint rows, no waiting, one statement. Add a locked_at and a reaper for crashed workers. 7. Prevention: Partial index on (id) WHERE status='pending'; a test with 20 concurrent workers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Redis locks for this; above roughly tens of thousands of jobs/s or fan-out needs, move to a real broker.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Worker dies mid-job? -> locked_at timeout plus reaper, jobs must be idempotent.
  • Strict ordering needed? -> SKIP LOCKED sacrifices strict order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue of invoices double-sent emails weekly until the select became FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Redis lock or ignores the race.
  • Hire: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a CTE.
  • Strong hire: adds reaper, partial index, idempotency and queue limits.

questions.promptHtml: Compare FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you can pick the least blocking lock and avoid FK-related contention.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: FOR UPDATE is the strongest: blocks other writers and lockers on the row. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is for updates that do not change key columns and does not block FK checks, which take FOR KEY SHARE; a normal UPDATE takes it automatically. FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE block writers but allow other sharers. NOWAIT errors immediately if locked; SKIP LOCKED ignores locked rows, ideal for queues.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
All hold until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, not statement end. Locking many rows writes xmax into each tuple, causing heap writes and WAL, so FOR UPDATE on a large range bloats and slows. Insert into a child table takes FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row, so FOR UPDATE on a parent row blocks child inserts but FOR NO KEY UPDATE does not.

BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• FOR UPDATE on huge ranges.
  • Taking locks in different orders in different paths.
  • Assuming the lock ends with the statement.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why NO KEY UPDATE? -> Avoids blocking child inserts doing FK checks on the parent.
  2. NOWAIT vs lock_timeout? -> NOWAIT fails instantly; lock_timeout waits up to a bound.
  3. Does FOR UPDATE lock rows added later? -> No; it locks only rows returned.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "FOR UPDATE locks the row". Senior: picks the weakest sufficient lock, ties to FK behaviour, and knows costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A parent-row FOR UPDATE in a billing job stalled child inserts across the fleet.

questions.contextHtml:
At 14:02 a deploy runs ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text; on a 60M-row table. Within 20 seconds the API returns 503s, the pool is exhausted at 200/200. Monitoring:

pg_stat_activity (state / wait):
 1 active   SELECT ... FROM users ... (running 8 min)    -- analytics export
 1 active   ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text      Lock: relation
 187 active SELECT/UPDATE users ...                        Lock: relation
CPU 12%, IOPS normal.

The team believes adding a nullable column is instant.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the outage and give the safe procedure.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The ALTER is slow because the table is big" (wrong: the column add is metadata only); "kill the ALTER" without knowing why.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which session holds the lock? What Postgres version? Can the export be killed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: pg_cancel_backend the ALTER (or terminate the export); queue clears immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ALTER waiting for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind the 8 minute export, and everyone queueing behind the ALTER; (b) table rewrite (not for a nullable column, red herring); (c) connection leak.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_blocking_pids chain: new queries -> ALTER -> export.
  5. Root cause: Lock queue. The ALTER itself needs milliseconds, but waiting for the strong lock makes all later requests wait behind it, even plain SELECTs.
  6. Fix: Procedure:
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text;   -- retry with backoff on timeout

Run when no long transactions exist, check pg_stat_activity first, and kill or reschedule long readers. 7. Prevention: statement_timeout for analytics roles, run exports on a replica, migration linter for lock timeout, alert on transactions older than N minutes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not removing the lock timeout to "make it succeed"; failing fast and retrying is safer than a freeze.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Column with default? -> Postgres 11+ constant default is metadata-only; volatile defaults rewrite.
  • ALTER on a replica set? -> Replicas replay the lock too and replay can stall behind long queries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A five-second ALTER caused a 10 minute incident because an analyst's laptop had a query open. Every migration then got lock_timeout by default.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames table size.
  • Hire: explains lock queue, uses lock_timeout.
  • Strong hire: adds replica exports, long-transaction alert, retry tooling.

questions.contextHtml:
A transfer endpoint moves money between two accounts. At 600 transfers/s, about 15 deadlocks per minute appear. Log excerpt:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 4417 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8801923; blocked by process 4421.
        Process 4421 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8801920; blocked by process 4417.
CONTEXT: while updating tuple (21,4) in relation "accounts"
STATEMENT: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2

Code: UPDATE accounts ... id = from; UPDATE accounts ... id = to;. The team wants to raise deadlock_timeout.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen and how do you remove it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase deadlock_timeout" or "retry only"; no ordering fix.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are transfers symmetric (A to B and B to A at once)? Do other paths touch accounts? Are transactions long?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Retry on 40P01 with jitter so users do not see errors.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) inconsistent lock order: A->B vs B->A; (b) a trigger or FK updating a third table in different order; (c) long transactions widen the window; (d) timeout setting (red herring, only changes detection delay).
  4. How I'd verify each: log_lock_waits=on, read both statements in the log; pg_stat_database.deadlocks rate.
  5. Root cause: Circular wait: T1 holds row 1 wanting row 2, T2 the reverse.
  6. Fix: Lock in a deterministic order:
BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
  1. Prevention: Code review rule: multi-row writes in key order; deadlock count alert; chaos test with reversed pairs.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising deadlock_timeout; it only delays detection and extends stalls.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Many rows per transaction? -> Sort the key list first.
  • Cannot order (external ids)? -> A coarse guard row or advisory lock, accepting less concurrency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settlement batch deadlocked nightly until sorted by id; the deadlock count went from hundreds to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes timeout.
  • Hire: consistent ordering plus retry.
  • Strong hire: reads the log precisely, adds monitoring and tests, discusses guard-lock fallback.

questions.promptHtml: What is a deadlock, how does Postgres handle it, and how is it different from a long lock wait?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can classify blocking problems correctly before fixing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A deadlock is a cycle of waits, A holds X wanting Y, B holds Y wanting X. After deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) Postgres finds the cycle, aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01 and the other proceeds. A long wait is a chain with no cycle: someone is just slow, and the timeout never aborts it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The deadlock check runs only after a process waits longer than deadlock_timeout, to avoid wasting CPU on short waits. It builds a wait-for graph from the lock table. Row locks waits appear as waiting on the holder's transaction id. Prevention order: consistent lock order, short transactions, lock the whole set up front in one ordered statement, retry. Diagnosis: log_lock_waits = on logs waits longer than deadlock_timeout; pg_stat_database.deadlocks counts them; pg_blocking_pids shows live chains.

A: UPDATE row1  ... UPDATE row2  (waits for B)
B: UPDATE row2  ... UPDATE row1  (waits for A)  -> cycle, one aborted

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling deadlocks a Postgres bug.
  • Treating a lock wait chain as a deadlock; the fix is a short transaction, not ordering.
  • Retrying without jitter, recreating the collision.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which transaction dies? -> The one whose check detects the cycle, typically the one that waited, not predictable.
  2. Can foreign keys cause deadlocks? -> Yes, via FOR KEY SHARE locks on parent rows.
  3. How does INSERT ... ON CONFLICT batching deadlock? -> Unordered batches take unique-key locks in different orders; sort by key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: define and say retry. Senior: classifies waits vs cycles, uses log and views, and designs ordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Batch upserts from two services deadlocked daily until both sorted by primary key.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly "close the books" job runs on one of 4 app instances. To avoid double runs it calls SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42) at start and pg_advisory_unlock(42) at the end, over PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. Two weeks in: some nights the job never runs (try_lock returns false on every instance), other nights it runs twice. pg_locks shows:

locktype  | objid | mode          | granted | pid
advisory  | 42    | ExclusiveLock | t       | 5523   (idle, connection in pool, no client)

Nobody holds the job now.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failures and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart Postgres" or "advisory locks are unreliable".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Pooling mode? Session or transaction? Is the job a single transaction? Can the job be long (hours)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(5523) to drop the leaked lock; or run pg_advisory_unlock_all() on that connection.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) session-level lock acquired on a pooled server connection, and the unlock call went through a different server connection (leaked on one, no-op on another); (b) job crash without unlock; (c) clock/cron skew (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Join pg_locks with pg_stat_activity on pid; compare pids at lock and unlock; check PgBouncer pool_mode.
  5. Root cause: In transaction pooling, consecutive statements from one client can go to different server connections. A session-level advisory lock belongs to the server connection, not the client, so it leaks or double-grants.
  6. Fix: Use a transaction-level lock inside one transaction: SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42) at the top of a single transaction that wraps the work or at least a short critical section; or use a dedicated direct connection for the lock; or a job_runs row with a unique key per date.
INSERT INTO job_runs(job, run_date) VALUES ('close_books', current_date)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id;   -- 1 row = I own today's run
  1. Prevention: Ban session-level advisory locks behind poolers; alert on idle connections holding advisory locks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A job_runs row also records history and survives crashes, at the cost of a stale-run policy (heartbeat).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Job lasts 3 hours, a transaction that long is bad? -> Use the job_runs row with heartbeat, not a lock held in a transaction.
  • Need cross-database mutual exclusion? -> etcd/ZooKeeper lease.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "run once" job ran twice and double-billed customers for an hour; the pooler change months earlier was the trigger.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart-based fixes.
  • Hire: spots session lock vs pooler, uses xact lock or run table.
  • Strong hire: heartbeat/expiry design and detection queries.

questions.promptHtml: Compare optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control and say when each is right.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Good engineers pick by conflict rate and think time, not habit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pessimistic locks first (FOR UPDATE) and prevents conflict; optimistic does no locking, remembers a version, and at write time updates only if the version is unchanged, retrying on zero rows. Use pessimistic for short transactions with frequent conflicts; use optimistic when conflicts are rare or when a human thinks between read and write, so no lock or transaction can stay open.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SELECT id, title, version FROM docs WHERE id = 5;       -- version = 7
UPDATE docs SET title = 'New', version = version + 1
WHERE id = 5 AND version = 7;                           -- 0 rows = conflict

JPA @Version, HTTP ETag with If-Match, DynamoDB conditional writes and etcd compare-and-swap are the same idea.

Pessimistic Optimistic
Best when Hot conflicts, short work Rare conflicts, long think time
Cost Waiting, deadlocks Retries
Holds DB state during user time Yes No
Failure mode Lock queues Retry storms on hot rows

For a hot counter, use neither: atomic SET n = n + 1, or shard the counter.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keeping a DB transaction open while a user fills a form.
  • Optimistic locking on a hot row.
  • Mixing both models on the same rows carelessly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you do on a conflict? -> Reload and merge or show a conflict message, depending on UX.
  2. Can xmin be a version? -> Technically, but an explicit column is portable and clear.
  3. Optimistic across microservices? -> ETag/If-Match or conditional writes on the owning service.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: picks by conflict rate and duration, mentions hot-row exceptions and retries.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An admin edit form held row locks through a connection pool and starved others; moving to version checks fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A video platform keeps videos.view_count updated per view: UPDATE videos SET view_count = view_count + 1 WHERE id=$1. At 500 views/s total it was fine. A viral video now gets 12,000 views/s on one row. Symptoms:

p99 latency of that endpoint 6 s; pool 100/100 busy
pg_stat_activity: 94 sessions wait_event Lock:transactionid (all updating id=9001)
WAL 40 MB/s; table videos has 3x bloat on hot pages

Other videos are fine. A teammate proposes optimistic locking with a version column.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now and what do you build for 10x?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Optimistic versioning (worse: almost every update retries) or "add a bigger instance".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must counts be exact in real time? Is it a display number or billing? How many hot rows exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed or batch writes for that id: buffer in the app/Redis and flush every second.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) single-row write serialization: each update waits for the previous to commit; (b) HOT chain bloat from 12k new versions per second on the same page; (c) pool exhaustion as a symptom, not a cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_blocking_pids chain on id 9001; n_dead_tup and pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd.
  5. Root cause: Every update to a row must wait for the prior holder; throughput per row is about 1 / (commit latency). Optimistic locking only adds retries.
  6. Fix: Short-term: write-behind aggregation. Long-term: an event table or sharded counters:
CREATE TABLE view_counter (video_id bigint, shard int, n bigint, PRIMARY KEY (video_id, shard));
INSERT INTO view_counter VALUES (9001, floor(random()*16)::int, 1)
ON CONFLICT (video_id, shard) DO UPDATE SET n = view_counter.n + 1;
SELECT sum(n) FROM view_counter WHERE video_id = 9001;

Roll up periodically. 7. Prevention: Load test with skewed keys; monitor top waiting rows. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharded counters make reads a sum; approximate counters are acceptable for display. Not optimistic locking.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exact billing counts? -> Append-only events, aggregate asynchronously.
  • Can unlogged tables help? -> They lose data on crash; only for disposable counters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A viral post took down an unrelated checkout path through the shared pool; separating pools per workload limited the blast radius.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: version column or vertical scaling.
  • Hire: batching or sharded counters.
  • Strong hire: explains per-row serialization math, bloat, and pool isolation.

questions.contextHtml: Orders table: 200 GB, 400M rows, 2,500 writes/s, zero downtime allowed. Required changes: (1) add index on user_id, (2) add CHECK (total >= 0), (3) add column channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web', (4) change status from varchar(20) to an enum. The index build takes about 30 minutes in staging.
questions.promptHtml: Give a step-by-step plan for each change with the lock each takes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Run plain ALTER/CREATE INDEX at night, or CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a migration transaction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Postgres version (11+ for instant defaults)? Replica lag tolerance? Is there a deploy tool that wraps migrations in a transaction? Rollback plan?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; plan is the work. First set lock_timeout and statement_timeout for migrations.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock queue; (b) a table rewrite; (c) long index build impacting I/O; (d) failed concurrent build leaving INVALID index.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_progress_create_index, pg_index.indisvalid, replica lag, pg_stat_activity for blockers.
  5. Root cause of danger: Many ALTER forms need ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; some rewrite 200 GB.
  6. Fix: Plan:
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
-- 1: weak lock, 2-3x longer, outside a transaction
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);
-- 2: cheap add, validate later (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_total CHECK (total >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_total;
-- 3: constant default is metadata only on PG 11+
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web';

Step 4: add a new column status_v2, dual write via app/trigger, backfill in batches of 10k with sleeps, switch reads, drop old; a direct type change rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. 7. Prevention: Migration linter (reject non-concurrent indexes, missing lock_timeout); rehearse on a restored copy. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Concurrent index build costs more I/O and can fail; check validity and drop invalid. Not doing the type change in place.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Build fails at 90%? -> INVALID index remains; drop concurrently and retry.
  • Replica lag from backfill? -> Smaller batches, pace on lag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "safe" nightly index build blocked writes for 40 minutes because the tool wrapped it in a transaction and fell back to the blocking form.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: plain DDL.
  • Hire: CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID/VALIDATE, lock_timeout.
  • Strong hire: dual-write backfill for the type change, invalid-index handling, lag pacing, linter.

questions.promptHtml: Does Postgres escalate row locks to table locks? Which operations take table-wide locks that surprise people?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mental model versus SQL Server/Db2, and awareness of foreign key and maintenance locks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Postgres stores row locks in the tuple header so there is no lock-table memory pressure to escalate from. But several operations take table locks: most ALTER TABLE forms (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE), CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY (blocks writes), VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, TRUNCATE, non-concurrent REINDEX. Foreign keys add row locks on parent rows, which can cause contention.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Row lock = xmax set plus flags, so locking 10M rows writes 10M tuple headers (heap writes and WAL) but never inflates to a table lock. SQL Server escalates around thousands of locks, which can freeze a table. FK: inserting into a child takes FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row; updates of parent non-key columns take FOR NO KEY UPDATE and do not conflict; deleting a parent scans the child (needs an index on the FK column) or it seq-scans under a lock.

Safe migration ordering
lock_timeout -> add column -> CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY -> NOT VALID -> VALIDATE

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction (error) or leaving INVALID indexes.
  • Missing index on FK child column.
  • Assuming type change is metadata only (usually a rewrite).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does VALIDATE CONSTRAINT lock? -> SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, writes continue.
  2. Why is a big FOR UPDATE still costly? -> It dirties pages and generates WAL.
  3. How avoid a rewrite for a type change? -> Expand/contract with a new column.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Postgres has row-level locking". Senior: no escalation, but the list of table-wide DDL locks, FK locking and mitigation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A missing FK index made parent deletes scan 300M child rows under lock and stall a nightly purge.

questions.contextHtml:
A payout service uses pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('merchant:'||id)) so only one worker pays a merchant at a time. A worker took the lock, then hit a 70 second GC pause while calling the bank API. Its transaction was killed by idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=30s; another worker took the lock and paid. The first worker woke up and its API call went through too. Merchant 5521 was paid twice (INR 4.2 lakh).

w1: lock acquired 02:00:01 ... pause ... bank call at 02:01:15 -> paid
w2: lock acquired 02:00:40 -> bank call at 02:00:42 -> paid
questions.promptHtml: What are the design flaws, and how do you make double payment impossible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout" or "use Redis Redlock".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the bank API support idempotency keys? Is the payout recorded before the call? What is the exactly-once expectation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Recover the money, freeze payouts for the merchant, reconcile with the bank file.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock does not protect the external side effect after it expires; (b) no idempotency key on the bank call; (c) long external I/O inside a lock transaction.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bank request logs; payout table rows per merchant per cycle.
  5. Root cause: A lock is only a lease. A paused process can resume believing it still holds it; the external system has no way to reject the stale holder.
  6. Fix: Make the effect idempotent and fenced:
-- one row per (merchant, cycle); unique key is the guard
INSERT INTO payouts(merchant_id, cycle, status) VALUES (5521, '2026-11-10', 'pending')
ON CONFLICT (merchant_id, cycle) DO NOTHING RETURNING id;

Send the payout id as the bank idempotency key, and update status via UPDATE ... WHERE status='pending'. A fencing token (monotonic number checked by the resource) covers resources that cannot take idempotency keys. 7. Prevention: No external I/O inside a lock transaction; reconciliation job; chaos test with paused workers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The lock stays only as an optimisation to reduce duplicate attempts. I would not trust any lease for correctness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bank has no idempotency? -> Pre-record intent, query bank by reference before retry, reconcile.
  • Why not Redlock? -> Still a lease; same pause problem.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A finance incident postmortem concluded "locks reduce, constraints decide"; every payout path got a unique business key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lengthens timeouts.
  • Hire: idempotency key and unique constraint.
  • Strong hire: explains leases, fencing tokens, outbox/recon, and keeps I/O out of the lock.

questions.contextHtml:
Two services, pricing-sync and inventory-sync, both bulk upsert into sku_stats (6M rows) with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE in batches of 5,000, concurrently, every 10 minutes. Since a data-source change, the jobs fail about 30% of the time:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 901 waits for ShareLock on transaction 77120044; blocked by process 877.
        Process 877 waits for ShareLock on transaction 77120037; blocked by process 901.
CONTEXT: while inserting index tuple (88213,5) in relation "sku_stats_pkey"

A previous fix attempt, retrying the whole job, made the job time 4x longer. Incident review asks for the root cause and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the jobs at different times" without explaining why it deadlocks, or lowering batch size only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the source ordering? Do both jobs touch overlapping skus? Is the batch one statement or many?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stagger schedules and cap concurrency for a few days.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) overlapping key sets processed in different orders; (b) large batch widens the lock window; (c) a missing index (red herring: the context shows the pkey).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the key order from both sources; take the log context for both processes.
  5. Root cause: Each statement locks keys in the order it processes them. Source A emits skus ascending, source B in arrival order, so A holds sku 10 wanting 20 while B holds 20 wanting 10.
  6. Fix: Sort each batch by sku before the upsert, and dedupe within the batch (ON CONFLICT cannot affect the same row twice in one command):
rows = sorted({r.sku: r for r in rows}.values(), key=lambda r: r.sku)
for chunk in chunks(rows, 1000):
    upsert(chunk)
  1. Prevention: Shared helper for bulk upserts, enforcing order; alert on pg_stat_database.deadlocks; test with reversed input.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Smaller batches reduce but do not remove the cycle. Not whole-job retries; retry only the failed batch with jitter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cannot sort across jobs? -> Single writer queue or advisory lock per shard of skus.
  • Duplicate sku in a batch? -> Error "cannot affect row a second time"; dedupe first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One shared bulk-write helper that sorted keys ended an entire class of nightly deadlocks across six services.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: schedules differently only.
  • Hire: consistent order, batch retry.
  • Strong hire: dedupe, shared helper, log reading, metrics and test.
